body_markdown:
What is an ASO and how does it differ from a PEO?
ASO, short for administrative services organization, is an industry term for a provider that takes on full administrative outsourcing of payroll and HR work. It is used loosely, and the IRS and the Department of Labor do not define it for payroll or HR. A professional employer organization (PEO) is a category the IRS describes, and the tax result follows the facts, such as who pays the wages and whose employer identification number (EIN) files the returns.
What does ASO mean, and what does the IRS say about it?
Because the term is used loosely, a provider’s use of it does not tell you what the provider does, who pays the wages or whose EIN files the returns.


The IRS’s third party arrangement chart compares payroll service providers, reporting agents, section 3504 agents and certified professional employer organizations (CPEOs) by form, filing EIN and liability. The chart has no category called ASO.
What is a PEO in the IRS’s words?
The IRS describes a PEO as an organization that performs some or all of a client’s federal employment tax withholding, reporting and payment functions, and says a PEO may also manage human resources, according to the Internal Revenue Manual on third-party payer arrangements. In industry usage, a PEO is described as a co-employment model. For federal tax purposes, the IRS says the Code does not define “co-employer” and the concept is not recognized under federal tax law.


The same manual says a PEO may represent itself to a client as the employer. A PEO that does cannot request authorization from the IRS as a reporting agent on Form 8655 or as a section 3504 agent on Form 2678.
What does the service-agreement test look at?
Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 defines a service agreement by three elements, and all three are required. The payor asserts that it is the employer or co-employer, pays the wages, and assumes responsibility for the taxes. The regulation uses the word co-employer only as one way a payor can assert that it is the employer.


A PEO that is not a CPEO and meets the service-agreement definition in Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 is designated to perform employer acts for the wages it pays, and the IRS says the PEO and its client are concurrently liable.


The designation does not apply when the wages are reported on a return filed under the client’s EIN. The regulation’s own example describes a payroll services provider that did not assert it was the employer and filed under the employer’s EIN. The regulation says that provider is not liable under that section, and the employer remains subject to employer law. The regulation also lists other exceptions, including a payor that is itself the employer of the individuals, and it does not apply to a payor authorized as an agent of the employer under Treasury Regulation 31.3504-1.


The same facts decide the result for a provider that uses the ASO label. When the provider asserts that it is the employer or co-employer, pays the wages and assumes responsibility for the taxes, it meets the three elements of the service-agreement definition, so the designation applies to the wages it pays, except where the regulation’s exceptions apply, such as wages reported on a return filed under the client’s EIN. When the provider does not assert employer status and files under the client’s EIN, it matches the regulation’s example instead.
What can a PEO be certified as?
A PEO can apply to become a CPEO. Congress added the CPEO program to the Internal Revenue Code in December 2014. Certification is voluntary, and the IRS certifies a PEO against tax, background, business-location, financial-audit and bond requirements.


Under Internal Revenue Code section 3511, a CPEO is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee. The IRS says certification may affect the employment tax liabilities of both the CPEO and its customers.
What does each arrangement change for federal employment taxes?
The table below sets out what the IRS says about each arrangement. Where the answer depends on the provider’s arrangement, the cell holds a question to ask in writing, and the last row consists of questions because the IRS does not define the label.


Arrangement
Employer for federal employment taxes
Who files
What the employer keeps
Payroll service provider or reporting agent
The employer. The IRS says neither the provider nor the reporting agent is liable as an employer or an agent for the employer’s employment taxes.
A payroll service provider prepares returns for the employer’s signature, and a reporting agent signs and generally e-files them, under the employer’s EIN.
Responsibility for returns, deposits and Forms W-2 and W-3.
PEO that is not a CPEO
In the arrangement the IRS describes, the client typically remains the common law employer. A payor under a service agreement is designated to perform employer acts for the wages it pays.
Under whose EIN will Forms 941, 940, W-2 and W-3 be filed?
The client remains subject to employer law, and the IRS says the client generally is not relieved of its employment tax obligation.
CPEO
The CPEO, for worksite employees and for pay it remits.
The CPEO reports wages under the CPEO’s EIN and allocates them to each customer by the customer’s EIN on Schedule R.
The customer may also be liable for employees who are not worksite employees.
Provider that uses the ASO label
Does the provider assert that it is the employer or co-employer, pay the wages and assume responsibility for the taxes?
Which IRS forms will be on file for you, such as Form 8655, Form 2678 or Form 8973?
How can you verify deposits yourself, and which address is the IRS address of record?
What can a contract not change?
The IRS says liability is set by the Internal Revenue Code and cannot be changed by a private agreement or contract.


The IRS says an employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes, with an exception for certified professional employer organizations, as Publication 15 explains. Where the employer remains responsible and the third party fails to make the deposits and payments, the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer’s account.

How should you describe a provider accurately before you sign?
Describe a provider by what it does, using the IRS’s terms, and put the answers in the contract. Beyond the questions in the last row of the table, ask these in writing.


* Ask whether the provider is a CPEO on the IRS list, and which exact legal name and EIN appear in the contract.
* Ask how wages will be allocated to your EIN on Schedule R, and how you will receive client-level reports.
* Ask what the base fee covers, which HR and benefits services are in scope, what service levels apply, how long implementation takes and what fees apply on exit.
Frequently asked questions
Is an ASO the same as a PEO?
The IRS describes the PEO category and does not define ASO for payroll or HR, so a provider’s tax treatment depends on the facts of its arrangement. Ask for those facts in writing rather than relying on either name.
Does a PEO have to be certified?
Certification is voluntary under the Internal Revenue Code. A PEO that is not certified is still subject to the service-agreement rule in Treasury Regulation 31.3504-2 when its agreement meets that definition.
Does using a PEO relieve an employer of payroll tax responsibility?
Generally not. IRS guidance to its own examiners says the client generally is not relieved of its employment tax obligation by using a PEO, and it tells examiners to advise the client to use due diligence in selecting and continuing with a PEO. The exception Publication 15 names is a CPEO, which is treated as the employer of a worksite employee for federal employment taxes, but only for pay the CPEO remits to that employee.
How can I check whether a provider is a CPEO?
Check the IRS’s published list of certified CPEOs, which the IRS updates quarterly and publishes with separate lists of suspended and revoked CPEOs. A CPEO contract must show the CPEO’s exact name and EIN, according to IRS guidance for CPEO customers, so compare the contract’s exact name with the entries on the list.
Does ASO have another meaning?
It does in health benefits, where the definitions federal surveys use spell ASO as administrative services only and describe an arrangement in which an employer hires a third party to deliver administrative services to the employer such as claims processing and billing, and the employer bears the risk for claims. That health plan arrangement is separate from the payroll and HR sense of the term.
